stem: A postpartum client had tearfulness and mood swings beginning a few days after birth that resolved without treatment within two weeks. Which interpretation is most accurate?
rationale: ACOG describes postpartum baby blues as mild, temporary mood symptoms that commonly begin about 2–3 days after childbirth and usually improve within a few days or 1–2 weeks without treatment. The timing, mild tearfulness/mood lability, and spontaneous resolution in this stem therefore support baby blues. Postpartum depression is more intense and impairs daily functioning, a persistent major depressive episode is inconsistent with this brief self-limited course, and postpartum psychosis would involve severe symptoms such as psychosis rather than isolated transient mood lability.
educational_objective: Differentiate postpartum baby blues from postpartum depression and more severe postpartum psychiatric disorders by their early onset, mild mood lability, and spontaneous resolution within about 1–2 weeks.
source_organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG)
source_locator: FAQ sections ‘What are the baby blues?’ and ‘How long do the baby blues usually last?’; glossary entry ‘Baby Blues’. Baby blues begin about 2–3 days after childbirth and usually improve within a few days or 1–2 weeks without treatment.
source_claim_supported: Transient tearfulness and mood swings beginning a few days postpartum and resolving spontaneously within 1–2 weeks are consistent with postpartum baby blues rather than postpartum depression.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — recognition of psychosocial adaptation, coping, emotional responses, and mental-health conditions in the postpartum period.
blueprint_topic: Psychosocial Integrity — postpartum mood adaptation and differentiation of baby blues from depressive illness

source_original.stem: A postpartum client had tearfulness and mood swings beginning a few days after birth that resolved without treatment within two weeks. Which interpretation is most accurate?
source_original.rationale: ACOG notes that postpartum baby blues commonly begin a few days after delivery and usually improve within days to one or two weeks without treatment. Option B fits the timing, mild symptoms, and spontaneous resolution. Option A and D describe depression despite a short, self-limited course. Option C is inconsistent with the absence of severe psychotic symptoms and the benign resolution.
source_original.source_detail: ACOG Postpartum Depression FAQ — Baby Blues: onset about 2–3 days postpartum and usually improve within a few days to 1–2 weeks without treatment. ACOG FAQ published 2024-04, last reviewed 2025-12; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Psychosocial Integrity; coping, support systems, grief/loss and therapeutic adaptation activities as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: No clinical correction was required. Source currentness and the exact ACOG FAQ locators were reverified; the rationale was tightened to distinguish the brief self-limited baby-blues course from depressive and psychotic disorders without adding unsupported diagnostic criteria.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current official ACOG patient guidance with explicit onset and duration criteria.
audit_findings.currentness: FAQ091 was published April 2024 and last reviewed December 2025; rechecked 2026-08-16.
audit_findings.exact_locator: The baby-blues FAQ sections directly support onset around 2–3 days postpartum and spontaneous improvement within a few days or 1–2 weeks.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The item uses only supported timing, mild mood symptoms, and spontaneous resolution; it does not add a universal symptom count, severity threshold, or treatment rule.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because the brief self-limited course is characteristic of baby blues rather than postpartum depression.
distractor_audit.B: Correct and directly matches ACOG timing and resolution.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because no psychotic symptoms or severe behavioral disturbance are present.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because a persistent major depressive episode is incompatible with symptoms resolving spontaneously within two weeks.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B fits the full timing, severity pattern, and spontaneous resolution described.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are postpartum mood/psychiatric interpretations and are concise without length cues.
audit_findings.blueprint: Fits Psychosocial Integrity through recognition of normal versus pathologic postpartum emotional responses.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Second-pass review checked whether a depressive episode could be defended at the two-week boundary; the stem specifies onset a few days postpartum and complete spontaneous resolution within two weeks, matching ACOG baby-blues guidance and excluding persistent depression.
